topic: Array new[] and delete[] Operators in C++
explanation: C++ provides separate operators for allocating and deallocating arrays: 'new[]' and 'delete[]', which are distinct from their single-object counterparts. The 'new[]' operator allocates memory for an array and constructs each element by calling the default constructor, storing metadata about the array size (implementation-dependent, often as a hidden size_t before the array). The 'delete[]' operator reads this metadata to determine how many destructors to call, then calls the destructor for each element in reverse order, and finally deallocates the memory. Critically, you must match 'new[]' with 'delete[]' and 'new' with 'delete' - mixing them causes undefined behavior because: (1) 'delete[]' expects array metadata that 'new' doesn't create, and (2) 'delete' won't call destructors for all array elements. Under the hood, 'new[]' calls 'operator new[]' (the array allocation function) and 'delete[]' calls 'operator delete[]' (the array deallocation function), both of which can be overloaded separately from their single-object versions. This design allows fine-grained control over array memory management but requires discipline to avoid mismatches that lead to memory corruption, leaks, or crashes.
example_explanation: This example demonstrates the critical difference between new[]/delete[] for arrays and new/delete for single objects. The Element class has custom operator new[] and operator delete[] to show when array allocation occurs. Using 'new Element[3]' allocates space for 3 elements plus metadata, constructs each one, and 'delete[]' destroys all 3 in reverse order then deallocates. The commented wrong examples show common mistakes: using 'delete' on an array only destroys one element and leaks the rest, while using 'delete[]' on a single object reads garbage as the array size causing crashes. You must match new[] with delete[] and new with delete.
